sources.note: Calls Chinantec 'un idioma sumamente nasal y tonal' (same segmental word, different meanings by tone) and describes a practical alphabet for Ojitlan/[second variant]/Valle Nacional that marks three tones: tono alto with an acute accent (ta with accent), tono bajo with an underline, tono medio unmarked; nasalization marked on the vowel. Implies at least a three-height lexical tone contrast written for Valle Nacional; no contour/sandhi detail visible.

sources.locator: printed p. 13, Introduction ch. 2 'Phonological Developments'; printed p. 31, Explanatory Notes, note 6; printed p. 8, ch. 1 'Dialect Variation'
sources.note: This work describes Proto Chinantec reconstruction plus tone reflexes for ten daughter languages (Ojitlan, Usila, Tlacoatzintepec, Sochiapan, Tepetotutla, Palantla, Lalana, Lealao, Quiotepec, Comaltepec); Valle Nacional (VN) appears only as a lexical-data poin. The work has no description of Valle Nacional word stress, accent or tone. VN is not among the five dialect areas with tonal data (note 6, p. 31); the tone-reflex tables of Appendix C (printed pp. 171-173, PDF 185-187) have rows for Oj, U, Tl, S, Tp, Pa, Ll, Le, Qi, Co only, no VN row; VN forms in the dictionary entries are cited witho…

tone.says: For Valle Nacional: tone is phonemic ('contrastive') but Rensch had no satisfactory analysis, so no tone inventory is given; syllables may be nasalized and/or checked by glottal stop; status of post-syllabic [ng] uncertain. (The preceding Ozumacin section says 'nasalization and obligatory tone are contrastive'.) This is the only first-hand published phonological statement on VN located.
